content: Exchange blood transfusion (EBT) is a medical procedure in which the entire blood volume of a newborn is replaced within a few hours. This intervention is commonly employed in neonatal medicine to manage severe anemia or significant hyperbilirubinemia during the first week of life. A notable complication associated with EBT is hypocalcemia, which is believed to result from the chelating properties of citrate, an anticoagulant frequently used in donor blood. Hypocalcemia can manifest as muscular and nervous irritability, as well as cardiac arrhythmias. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether the administration of prophylactic intravenous calcium could reduce the risk of hypocalcemia-related complications and mortality in newborns undergoing EBT. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard strategy. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched up to June 29, 2016. Additional sources, including clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles, were also reviewed to identify randomized and quasi-randomized trials. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized and quasi-randomized trials investigating the use of prophylactic intravenous calcium during EBT in neonates. Two independent reviewers assessed and extracted data on study methods, participant characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. Outcomes of interest included total and ionized serum calcium levels before and after EBT, as well as adverse events such as hypoglycemia, apnea, cardiac arrest, and mortality immediately following the procedure. Data were analyzed using mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes and risk ratios (RR) and risk differences (RD) with 95% CIs for dichotomous outcomes. The quality of evidence was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and the GRADE system. The review identified only one quasi-randomized trial involving 30 participants that met the inclusion criteria. In this study, total and ionized serum calcium levels were measured immediately before and after EBT. All participants were included in the final analysis, and all key outcomes were reported. For primary outcomes, there was one death in each group (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 14.55; RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.18). The study did not report the incidence of cardiac arrhythmias within one week of EBT or the number of infants with serum calcium levels below critical thresholds (total calcium <8 mg/dL or ionized calcium <4.4 mg/dL). A comparison of EBT with intravenous 10% calcium gluconate versus EBT without calcium showed that mean total serum calcium levels increased in the intervention group compared to the control group (MD -0.46, 95% CI -0.81 to -0.11). Similarly, very low-quality evidence suggested an increase in mean ionized serum calcium levels in the intervention group (MD -0.22, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.11). For secondary outcomes, adverse reactions to intravenous calcium therapy included one case of cardiac arrest in the intervention group (RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.13 to 68.26; RD 0.07, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.23). Apnea and hypoglycemia were observed in the two neonates who died (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 14.55; RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.18). Data on other secondary outcomes, such as reduced serum magnesium, altered parathormone or calcitonin levels, seizures, carpopedal spasm, jitteriness, and prolonged QTc interval on electrocardiography, were not available. The authors concluded that very low-quality evidence from a single quasi-randomized trial suggested an increase in mean total and ionized serum calcium levels in the intervention group compared to the control group immediately after EBT. However, the mean calcium levels in both groups remained within international reference ranges. Importantly, data were insufficient to evaluate trends in calcium levels during the first week following EBT. Given the limited and low-quality evidence, it is challenging to definitively support or refute the routine use of prophylactic intravenous calcium in newborns undergoing EBT. The authors emphasized the need for well-designed, larger-scale trials to address this question, particularly focusing on differences based on gestational age, the type of anticoagulant used, and the volume of blood exchanged.
